items.followUp: Define the axis of rotation of a spinning wheel.

rubric.why: The definition must identify the axis as an imaginary line about which a body rotates.
rubric.description: Defines the axis of rotation.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear definition containing both ideas.

modelAnswer: The axis of rotation is the imaginary line about which a body rotates.

items.followUp: State the approximate value of g on Earth and on the Moon.

rubric.description: Gives the value of g on Earth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct value.

rubric.why: The value on the Moon is approximately 1.6 m s⁻².
rubric.description: Gives the value of g on the Moon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct value.

modelAnswer: On the Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻².

items.followUp: Define mechanical energy and give an example of a body that possesses it.

rubric.why: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.
rubric.description: Defines mechanical energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.

rubric.why: A freely falling body is an example of a body with mechanical energy.
rubric.description: Gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example.

modelAnswer: Mechanical energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of a body.
Example: A freely falling body possesses mechanical energy.

items.followUp: What happens to the elastic potential energy of a spring when it is stretched?

rubric.why: Elastic potential energy is stored energy.
rubric.description: Identifies it as stored energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is stored.

rubric.why: The energy is stored in an elastic body when its shape changes due to stretching or compression.
rubric.description: Links the stored energy to deformation of an elastic body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning stretching, compression, or change of shape.

modelAnswer: Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in an elastic body when it is stretched or compressed.

items.followUp: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as we go higher above the Earth?

rubric.why: Atmospheric pressure changes with altitude.
rubric.description: Identifies the effect of increasing height.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure decreases with increasing height.

rubric.why: At greater height, there is less air above and therefore less weight of air pressing down.
rubric.description: Explains the change in pressure in terms of the air above.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the weight or amount of air above decreases with height.

modelAnswer: As height increases, the amount of air above a point decreases.
Therefore, the weight of the air pressing down decreases, so atmospheric pressure decreases.

items.followUp: Derive the third equation of motion using a speed-time graph.

rubric.why: The displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, which is a trapezium.
rubric.description: Relates displacement to the area under the graph.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the trapezium-area expression or equivalent explanation.

rubric.why: The first equation of motion is used to eliminate final velocity.
rubric.description: States the first equation of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for v = u + at.

rubric.why: Substituting v = u + at into the displacement expression gives this intermediate step.
rubric.description: Substitutes for v in the displacement expression.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution and simplification.

rubric.why: This is the required second equation of motion.
rubric.description: Obtains the second equation of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final equation.

modelAnswer: From the speed-time graph, displacement s equals the area of the trapezium.
s = ½(u + v)t
Using the first equation of motion, v = u + at.
Substituting: s = ½(u + u + at)t
s = ½(2u + at)t
Therefore, s = ut + ½at²

items.followUp: A 10 g bullet is fired at 200 m s⁻¹ from a stationary 4 kg gun. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.

rubric.why: The bullet mass must be converted to SI units.
rubric.description: Converts the bullet mass to kilograms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the bullet mass as 0.02 kg.

rubric.why: The gun and bullet are initially at rest, so their total initial momentum is zero and momentum is conserved.
rubric.description: Applies conservation of momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct conservation statement or initial momentum.

rubric.why: The momentum equation must be set up with the bullet and gun momenta in opposite directions.
rubric.description: Substitutes the data into the momentum equation.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct equation and substitution; award 1 mark if the setup is substantially correct but has a minor error.

rubric.why: The negative sign indicates recoil opposite to the bullet's motion; the recoil speed is 0.4 m s⁻¹.
rubric.description: Gives the recoil velocity with direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 0.4 m s⁻¹ opposite to the bullet's motion.

modelAnswer: Given: Bullet mass, mᵦ = 20 g = 0.02 kg; bullet velocity, vᵦ = 100 m s⁻¹; gun mass, m𝗀 = 5 kg; initial momentum = 0.
By the law of conservation of momentum, mᵦvᵦ + m𝗀v𝗀 = 0.
Substitution: (0.02 kg)(100 m s⁻¹) + (5 kg)v𝗀 = 0.
The gun recoils at 0.4 m s⁻¹ opposite to the bullet's motion.

items.followUp: Define torque and explain how a couple turns a double-arm spanner.

rubric.why: Torque describes the turning effect of a force.
rubric.description: Defines torque.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying torque as the turning effect of a force.

rubric.why: Torque equals force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action.
rubric.description: Gives the mathematical equation for torque.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or equivalent statement.

rubric.why: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces acting at different points.
rubric.description: Describes the forces forming a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the forces are equal and opposite.

rubric.why: The separated forces on the double-arm spanner produce a turning effect; the couple's moment is one force times the perpendicular separation of their lines of action.
rubric.description: Explains the spanner example and the moment of a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the forces turn the spanner and identifying their separation as the couple arm.

modelAnswer: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a pivot or axis.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (τ = Fd).
A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces acting at different points.
When these forces are applied to the two arms of a double-arm spanner, they turn the spanner.
The moment of the couple equals one force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces.
